newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi refugee chief says killings special case.
newsitem.headline: Burundi refugee chief says killings special case.

text.p: The head of the U.N. refugee agency in Burundi on Monday described the massacre of at least 122 refugees by Burundian troops as a "special and particular case".
The victims, all Burundians, were expelled by Tanzanian authorities last Friday, accused of taking part in violence in their camps, and were killed the same day.

"I think it is a special and particular case because they were expelled by the Tanzanian army for being implicated in violent confrontations in the camps which caused eight deaths," Hitoshi Mise, head of the UNHCR in Burundi, told reporters.
A spokesman for Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army said on Saturday that troops shot dead all 126 of the refugees when they tried to escape from a detention centre.
Mise said four of the 126 from Kitale camp in fact survived.
Burundi is at war between the army and Hutu rebels fighting for a greater political stake in the tiny tea and coffee-growing country.
There are more than 80,000 Burundian Hutu refugees in Tanzania, mostly in the northwest close to the border.
An internal UNHCR document obtained by Reuters said a Tanzanian army truck transported the 126 refugees to Kobero, Burundi, at about one p.m. on January 10.
"All 126...were reportedly summarily shot at Kobero, Muyinga Province, by receiving Burundi military authorities," the document said.

This conflicted with a report on Burundi state radio last Saturday that the expelled refugees arrived at night and were a threat to outnumbered troops. Burundi's army says it has arrested seven soldiers.
Despite the massacre, Tanzania assured Burundian refugees they could go home in safety.

"The government asked Burundian refugees who are ready to go home not to hesitate to do so, because the situation in Burundi is not as threatening as is reported by certain quarters, although political disagreements continue," Tanzanian state radio reported on Sunday.
Tanzania, traditionally a safe haven for African refugees, ordered 500,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees to go home late last year. About 400,000 have already been obliged to leave.
U.N. human rights officials say more than 2,000 have since been arrested in Rwanda for their alleged role in the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994.
The leaked UNHCR document, dated last Saturday, raised fears about the fate of another 48 Burundian Hutu refugees who were "surrendered to a Burundi delegation" on January 5.
The agreement was they would not be harmed, it said.
"However it appears from credible sources the contrary did take place," the document said, without elaboration.
The UNHCR says Kitale camp has witnessed factional fighting between rival Hutu rebels since December. U.N. officials say more than 10 refugees have died in clashes.
Mise said last weekend the fighting pitted members of Palepehutu against elements of the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD).
Mise said all the expelled were members of the Palepehutu, Burundi's oldest active Hutu rebel movement.
